proposals.relationship: Farge credits Foucault’s writings with turning her historical practice toward ruptures and discontinuities, and his analysis of power with opening an inquiry into popular opinion.
proposals.evidence_note: Farge’s own 2012 answer identifies the effect on her practice. Her 17 June 1997 interview specifies La Volonté de savoir and Surveiller et punir when explaining the archival investigation behind Dire et mal dire. This is an acknowledged resource, distinct from joint authorship and from her particular disagreement over presenting documents. The complete cited books were not freshly read.
primary_locators: Ortiz, 29 May 2012, Farge’s answer to the question on the subaltern, after her 13/14 July 1789 example.
Kouvelakis interview, first Farge answer beginning Avant de répondre à la dernière question, public article-record paragraph 2.

proposals.relationship: Farge recalls opposing Foucault’s initial wish to present the documents for Le Désordre des familles without commentary: their aesthetic force still required historical explanation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2001 recollection of their work on the jointly credited 1982 book. She explicitly shares his emotional response to the documents; the disagreement concerns their initial presentation. It establishes neither a rejection of Foucault nor the book’s final division of labor. The original editorial conversation and complete book remain unread.
primary_locators: Le siècle mineur, answer to question contrasting Foucault’s La vie des hommes infâmes with Farge’s warnings about literature; article-body paragraph 37; n 9 gives the jointly authored 1982 book.

proposals.relationship: Farge explicitly uses Bourdieu’s Méditations pascaliennes to examine bodies as sites where political power is inscribed and collective action becomes possible.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2001 response about bodily experience names this particular analytical resource. The book itself remains unread in this dossier. Her specific criticism of La Domination masculine is separately retained; use of one argument does not establish agreement with all of Bourdieu’s work.
primary_locators: Le siècle mineur, paragraph beginning Pour ça, j’ai beaucoup utilisé Bourdieu, article-body paragraph 24; n 11 identifies Méditations pascaliennes, 1997; paragraph 30 returns to connaissance par corps.

proposals.relationship: Farge includes Bourdieu’s La Domination masculine in her criticism of accounts that make gender domination invariant, while directing the sharper objection at Françoise Héritier.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2001 answer contrasts historical movement with invariance and names Bourdieu’s 1998 book. The main target remains Héritier’s Masculin/Féminin; she is not replaced by Bourdieu. Existing field edge 1402 already preserves that broader intervention and remains unchanged. Neither original book was freshly read.
primary_locators: Le siècle mineur, response to the Héritier question, article-body paragraphs 8–9, especially the comparison with La Domination masculine; nn 5–6 distinguish the 1996 and 1998 books.

proposals.relationship: Farge identifies Habermas’s account of a repressed plebeian public sphere as an intellectual stimulus for investigating popular political judgment in Dire et mal dire.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview dated Paris, 17 June 1997, preserved in the publisher’s public article record. She calls Habermas’s formulation a stimulus while explaining the different historical investigation it prompted. Complete L’Espace public and Dire et mal dire were not read here. The resource coexists with her explicit historical objections.
primary_locators: Kouvelakis interview, first Farge answer beginning Avant de répondre à la dernière question; first subparagraph, API article 422, rendered paragraph 2; interviewer’s opening quotations from Dire et mal dire p 13 are distinguished from her own answer.

proposals.relationship: Farge challenges a history of public opinion that leaves popular judgment uncultured or merely repressed and makes change descend continuously from the literate bourgeois sphere.
proposals.evidence_note: Her 17 June 1997 answers explicitly limit this to historical inquiry, disclaiming a direct philosophical critique of Habermas. She investigates changing practices, intermediate relays and discontinuities. This does not assert that Habermas denied every plebeian sphere. The response is read in the publisher’s transcription, not the complete 1992 monograph; the transmission contains unresolved corruptions outside the cited sentences.
primary_locators: Kouvelakis interview, first Farge answer (rendered paragraph 2), answer beginning Voyez, vous dites Le peuple pense (paragraph 12), and final answer’s subparagraph beginning Quant à la vision habermassienne (paragraph 16).

proposals.relationship: In her 2013 foreword, Davis treats Farge’s account of archival work as a guide that deepens her own understanding of research, interpretation and the material encounter with documents.
proposals.evidence_note: Davis’s own selected foreword, especially xii–xv, not evidence of formative influence on her earlier career. Her coediting recollection on x establishes collaboration without causal priority. Thomas Scott-Railton translated Farge’s 1989 book; Davis wrote the separate 2013 foreword. The legal preview ends during xv; the complete foreword and Farge’s book body remain unread.
primary_locators: Natalie Zemon Davis, Foreword to The Allure of the Archives (2013), xii–xv; xiii visually collated, with x checked for joint editorial credit.
